q: You cannot step twice into the same rivers; for fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you.
note: The river stays the same river only because new water keeps flowing through it. Identity lives on change.

q: Wantonness needs putting out, even more than a house on fire.
note: Hubris, arrogant excess, spreads like fire and destroys more. Put it out first.

q: The bow (βιός) is called life (βίος) but its work is death.
note: A pun in Greek: biós (bow) and bíos (life). The name says life, the thing deals death.

q: Of all whose discourses I have heard, there is not one who attains to understanding that wisdom is apart from all.
note: Wisdom is set apart from everything else people chase, and almost nobody notices that.

q: It is the opposite which is good for us.
note: We are helped by what differs from us. Contrast makes things work.

q: Hesiod is most men’s teacher. Men are sure he knew very many things, a man who did not know day or night! They are one.
note: Hesiod made Day and Night separate beings. Heraclitus: they are one process with two phases.

q: It is pleasure to souls to become moist.
note: For Heraclitus, a wet soul is a soul in decline. Pleasure can be the downhill slope.

q: Those who speak with understanding must hold fast to what is common to all as a city holds fast to its law, and even more strongly. For all human laws are fed by the one divine law. It prevails as much as it will, and suffices for all things with something to spare.
note: Reason is shared the way a city’s law is shared, and every human law draws on one deeper law.

q: Time is a child playing draughts, the kingly power is a child’s.
note: Time, or a lifetime, is a child at a board game. What rules the world is at play.

q: We must know that war is common to all and strife is justice, and that all things come into being and pass away (?) through strife.
note: Strife is not a breakdown of order. It is the order.

q: The lord whose is the oracle at Delphoi neither utters nor hides his meaning, but shows it by a sign.
note: Apollo neither states nor conceals; he hints. Heraclitus writes the same way, and leaves the reading to you.

q: The many do not take heed of such things as those they meet with, nor do they mark them when they are taught, though they think they do.
note: Meeting something every day is not the same as understanding it. Familiarity passes itself off as knowledge.

q: To God all things are fair and good and right, but men hold some things wrong and some right.
note: From the whole, everything fits. Only from inside a part do things look wrong.

q: Gods and men honour those who are slain in battle.
note: The old Greek ideal: those who fall in battle are honoured on earth and among the gods.

q: Those who seek for gold dig up much earth and find a little.
note: Wisdom takes digging. Most of the effort turns up dirt; what you find is small, but it is gold.

q: The way of man has no wisdom, but that of God has.
note: Human ways of seeing fall short. Wisdom belongs to the whole, not to the part.

q: And it is law, too, to obey the counsel of one.
note: Following the advice of one wise person can be law too. Heraclitus was no democrat.

q: The eyes are more exact witnesses than the ears.
note: Seeing for yourself beats hearsay.

q: Knowing not how to listen nor how to speak.
note: Understanding starts with listening well. Only then is speaking worth anything.

q: All things are an exchange for Fire, and Fire for all things, even as wares for gold and gold for wares.
note: Fire works like money: everything can be traded for it and it for everything. One currency under all change.

q: When they are born, they wish to live and to meet with their dooms—or rather to rest—and they leave children behind them to meet with their dooms in turn.
note: Born, people want to live, then to rest, and they hand the same cycle on to their children.

q: One day is like any other.
note: Against lucky and unlucky days: every day has the same nature.

q: The sun will not overstep his measures; if he does, the Erinyes, the handmaids of Justice, will find him out.
note: Even the sun keeps to its limits. Cosmic order and moral order are one and the same.

q: A man may be a grandfather in thirty years.
note: Generations turn quickly. Human time runs in cycles.

q: The people must fight for its law as for its walls.
note: Law holds a community together as surely as its walls do. Defend both.

q: Man’s character is his fate.
note: êthos anthrópōi daimōn. What happens to you flows from who you are.

q: I have sought for myself.
note: Also read as “I searched myself.” Self-inquiry as the way to the Word.

q: Though this Word is true evermore, yet men are as unable to understand it when they hear it for the first time as before they have heard it at all. For, though all things come to pass in accordance with this Word, men seem as if they had no experience of them, when they make trial of words and deeds such as I set forth, dividing each thing according to its kind and showing how it truly is. But other men know not what they are doing when awake, even as they forget what they do in sleep.
note: Ancient sources say his book opened like this: the order is always there, yet most people walk through their days as if asleep.

q: Dogs bark at every one they do not know.
note: People attack what they don’t recognise.

q: The dry soul is the wisest and best.
note: A dry, fiery soul sees most clearly. Keep the fire going.

q: . . . (The wise man) is not known because of men’s want of belief.
note: Wisdom goes unnoticed because people don’t believe it is there.

q: Men would not have known the name of justice if these things were not.
note: Without injustice, nobody would have a word for justice. Concepts lean on their opposites.

q: Asses would rather have straw than gold.
note: Value depends on who is valuing. To a donkey, straw wins.

q: Man is called a baby by God, even as a child by a man.
note: To god, a grown man is a baby. A lesson in humility about our own cleverness.

q: It is not good for men to get all they wish to get. It is sickness that makes health pleasant; evil, good; hunger, plenty; weariness, rest.
note: Getting everything you want is not good for you. Contrast is what gives things their value.

q: Wisdom is one thing. It is to know the thought by which all things are steered through all things.
note: Real wisdom is a single insight: seeing the intelligence that steers everything through everything.

q: The straight and the crooked path of the fuller’s comb is one and the same.
note: The cloth-worker’s tool moves straight and turns at once. One motion, two descriptions.

q: The most esteemed of them knows but fancies, and holds fast to them, yet of a truth justice shall overtake the artificers of lies and the false witnesses.
note: Even the respected know only appearances. Liars get caught in the end.

q: The mysteries practised among men are unholy mysteries.
note: A critique of the secret religious rites of his day, as they were actually practised.

q: Every beast is driven to pasture with blows.
note: Every creature is driven along by force. Some read Zeus’s blow behind it; others a jab at people who only move when pushed.

q: Fire is want and surfeit.
note: Fire is always hungry and always overflowing, consuming and producing at once.

q: Couples are things whole and things not whole, what is drawn together and what is drawn asunder, the harmonious and the discordant. The one is made up of all things, and all things issue from the one.
note: Whole and part, harmony and discord belong together. Out of all things one, and out of one all things.

q: Fire lives the death of air, and air lives the death of fire; water lives the death of earth, earth that of water.
note: Each element lives by another’s death. The world is a chain of transformations, not a pile of stable things.

q: . . . the seasons that bring all things.
note: The seasons deliver everything in its turn. Time brings change in regular measure.

q: Eyes and ears are bad witnesses to men if they have souls that understand not their language.
note: The senses only help a mind that can read them. Perception without understanding is just noise.

q: War is the father of all and the king of all; and some he has made gods and some men, some bond and some free.
note: “War” here is the clash of opposites. Conflict is not only destructive; it is what sorts out who becomes what.

q: The waking have one common world, but the sleeping turn aside each into a world of his own.
note: Awake, we share one world. Asleep, each slips into a private one. Private worlds are a kind of sleep.

q: The Ephesians would do well to hang themselves, every grown man of them, and leave the city to beardless lads; for they have cast out Hermodoros, the best man among them, saying, “We will have none who is best among us; if there be any such, let him be so elsewhere and among others.”
note: A furious rant against his hometown, which exiled its best man for being the best. Envy dressed up as equality.

q: It is a weariness to labour for the same masters and be ruled by them.
note: Endless sameness wears you out. Change is relief, not threat.

q: Physicians who cut, burn, stab, and rack the sick, demand a fee for it which they do not deserve to get.
note: Doctors hurt in order to heal. Harm and help can be the very same act.

q: Corpses are more fit to be cast out than dung.
note: Once the fire of the soul is gone, the body is worth less than manure. A blunt jab at funeral piety.

q: If all things were turned to smoke, the nostrils would distinguish them.
note: If the world were all smoke, we would tell things apart by smell. Knowing adapts to whatever form things take.

q: They are estranged from that with which they have most constant intercourse.
note: We are strangers to what we deal with most. The order is everywhere, and still unfamiliar.

q: They vainly purify themselves by defiling themselves with blood, just as if one who had stepped into the mud were to wash his feet in mud. Any man who marked him doing thus, would deem him mad.
note: Washing off blood with blood is washing mud with mud. Empty ritual cleans nothing.

q: A man, when he gets drunk, is led by a beardless lad, tripping, knowing not where he steps, having his soul moist.
note: Drunk, a grown man has to be led by a boy. Lose control and you lose the soul’s fire.

q: Souls smell in Hades.
note: A strange one. Perhaps souls in the underworld, being smoke-like, perceive by smell.

q: It scatters and it gathers; it advances and retires.
note: Gathering and dispersing, advancing and retreating: the steady rhythm of a world in motion.

q: The wisest man is an ape compared to God, just as the most beautiful ape is ugly compared to man.
note: Ape is to man as man is to god. What we call excellence is relative.

q: Homer should be turned out of the lists and whipped, and Archilochos likewise.
note: No respect for the poets everyone revered. Fame is not wisdom.

q: In Priene lived Bias, son of Teutamas, who is of more account than the rest. (He said, “Most men are bad.”)
note: Bias of Priene, one of the Seven Sages, gets rare praise from Heraclitus, perhaps for that blunt verdict.

q: Cold things become warm, and what is warm cools; what is wet dries, and the parched is moistened.
note: Opposites keep turning into each other. Warm and cold are not fixed things but stages.

q: If there were no sun it would be night, for all the other stars could do.
note: All the stars together cannot make a day. One source makes the difference.

q: For it is death to souls to become water, and death to water to become earth. But water comes from earth; and from water, soul.
note: The soul is one stage in the cycle of the elements: soul to water to earth, and back again.

q: One is ten thousand to me, if he be the best.
note: One excellent person outweighs ten thousand. Quality over numbers.

q: The way up and the way down is one and the same.
note: Same road, seen from different ends.

q: We step and do not step into the same rivers; we are and are not.
note: The river again, and now it is us: from moment to moment we are and are not the same.

q: You will not find the boundaries of soul by travelling in any direction, so deep is the measure of it.
note: Walk any road you like, you will not reach the edge of the soul. The inner world has no border.

q: There awaits men when they die such things as they look not for nor dream of.
note: Whatever comes after death, it is not what anyone expects.

q: The transformations of Fire are, first of all, sea; and half of the sea is earth, half whirlwind. . . .
note: Fire becomes sea, sea becomes earth and fiery storm. Everything is fire at some stage of its change.

q: It is wise to hearken, not to me, but to my Word, and to confess that all things are one.
note: The Word (logos) is the pattern running through everything. Trust the pattern, not the speaker’s authority.

q: And the Sibyl, with raving lips uttering things mirthless, unbedizened, and unperfumed, reaches over a thousand years with her voice, thanks to the god in her.
note: No charm, no ornament, and still her voice carries a thousand years. Truth does not need to be pretty to last.

q: And they pray to these images, as if one were to talk with a man’s house, knowing not what gods or heroes are.
note: Praying to a statue is like chatting with a house. Whatever the gods are, they are not stone.

q: Fire in its advance will judge and convict all things.
note: Fire as judge: in the end, everything is tested by it.

q: All the things we see when awake are death, even as all we see in slumber are sleep.
note: Obscure. Perhaps: waking sight shows only fixed, dead things, as dreams show only sleep. The living process stays unseen.

q: It is hard to fight with one’s heart’s desire. Whatever it wishes to get, it purchases at the cost of soul.
note: Passion is hard to fight, and whatever it gets, it pays for with soul.

q: Oxen are happy when they find bitter vetches to eat.
note: What counts as good depends on the creature. Bitter weeds are a feast for an ox.

q: Those who are asleep are fellow-workers (in what goes on in the world).
note: Even sleepers help make what happens. Nobody stands fully outside the order.

q: It becomes liquid sea, and is measured by the same tale as before it became earth.
note: The books balance: whatever turns to sea and earth keeps its measure. Nothing is lost in the exchange.

q: And it is the same thing in us that is quick and dead, awake and asleep, young and old; the former are shifted and become the latter, and the latter in turn are shifted and become the former.
note: Living and dead, awake and asleep, young and old: one thing turning into its opposite and back.

q: It is not meet to act and speak like men asleep.
note: Don’t sleepwalk. Waking up is the task.

q: How can one hide from that which never sets?
note: The sun sets; what never sets is the ever-living fire, the order of things. Nobody slips out from under it.

q: Pythagoras, son of Mnesarchos, practised scientific inquiry beyond all other men, and making a selection of these writings, claimed for his own wisdom what was but a knowledge of many things and an imposture.
note: A swipe at Pythagoras: wide reading plus borrowed ideas, sold as wisdom.

q: In the circumference of a circle the beginning and end are common.
note: On a circle, start and finish are the same point.

q: This world, which is the same for all, no one of gods or men has made; but it was ever, is now, and ever shall be an ever-living Fire, with measures of it kindling, and measures going out.
note: No creator and no beginning: the world is an eternal fire, flaring up and dying down in fixed measures.

q: The sea is the purest and the impurest water. Fish can drink it, and it is good for them; to men it is undrinkable and destructive.
note: The same water is life for fish and death for people. Good and bad depend on who is involved.

q: Men do not know how what is at variance agrees with itself. It is an attunement of opposite tensions, like that of the bow and the lyre.
note: A bow or a lyre works because opposite pulls hold each other. Harmony is tension in balance, not its absence.

q: Thought is common to all.
note: Everyone shares the power to think. Insight is not private property.

q: The wise is one only. It is unwilling and willing to be called by the name of Zeus.
note: The one wisdom both fits and resists the name of god. Our words for the divine are true, but only partly.

q: The hidden attunement is better than the open.
note: The deepest order is not on display. What shows is the lesser harmony.

q: Nature loves to hide.
note: Physis, the real nature of a thing, does not sit on the surface. It has to be uncovered.

q: If you do not expect the unexpected, you will not find it; for it is hard to be sought out and difficult.
note: Insight comes to those who stay open to surprise. What you already expect, you have already limited.

q: Homer was wrong in saying: “Would that strife might perish from among gods and men!” He did not see that he was praying for the destruction of the universe; for, if his prayer were heard, all things would pass away. . . .
note: Wish strife away and you wish the world away. The tension between opposites is what keeps it alive.

q: Good and ill are one.
note: Not that good and evil are the same, but that they are bound together: each only makes sense with the other.

q: The sun is new every day.
note: He likely meant it literally: a fresh sun kindled each morning. Either way, nothing returns quite the same.

q: Let us not conjecture at random about the greatest things.
note: The biggest questions deserve the most careful thinking, not the loosest.

q: It is the thunderbolt that steers the course of all things.
note: The thunderbolt is Zeus’s weapon and pure fire. The intelligence that guides the world, pictured as lightning.

q: Fools when they do hear are like the deaf: of them does the saying bear witness that they are absent when present.
note: Hearing without understanding is a kind of absence. You can be in the room and still miss everything.

q: The things that can be seen, heard, and learned are what I prize the most.
note: Against empty speculation: experience comes first, as long as it is understood.

q: It is best to hide folly; but it is hard in times of relaxation, over our cups.
note: Hide your foolishness, if you can. Wine makes that hard.

q: It rests by changing.
note: Stability comes from motion, as in a flame or a river.

q: Men that love wisdom must be acquainted with very many things indeed.
note: Read it next to fragment 16: a lover of wisdom must know a great deal, though knowing a great deal is not yet wisdom.

q: The learning of many things teacheth not understanding, else would it have taught Hesiod and Pythagoras, and again Xenophanes and Hekataios.
note: Piling up information is not insight. The most famous know-it-alls of his day still missed the point.

q: The limit of dawn and evening is the Bear; and opposite the Bear is the boundary of bright Zeus.
note: Old sky-lore: the Great Bear marks where east meets west. Even the heavens are ruled by boundaries.

q: Swine wash in the mire, and barnyard fowls in dust.
note: Pigs bathe in mud, hens in dust. What counts as clean depends on who is getting clean.

q: Greater deaths win greater portions.
note: A nobler death earns a nobler lot.

q: For what thought or wisdom have they? They follow the poets and take the crowd as their teacher, knowing not that there are many bad and few good. For even the best of them choose one thing above all others, immortal glory among mortals, while most of them are glutted like beasts.
note: The crowd learns from poets and from itself. The best choose lasting glory over comfort.

q: So we must follow the common, yet though my Word is common, the many live as if they had a wisdom of their own.
note: The Word belongs to everyone, yet most live as if they had a private truth.

q: God is day and night, winter and summer, war and peace, surfeit and hunger; but he takes various shapes, just as fire, when it is mingled with spices, is named according to the savour of each.
note: God is the unity of all opposites, called by different names the way incense is named by its scent.

q: For if it were not to Dionysos that they made a procession and sang the shameful phallic hymn, they would be acting most shamelessly. But Hades is the same as Dionysos in whose honour they go mad and rave.
note: The god of wild life and the god of the dead are one. Frenzy and death belong together.

q: Even the posset separates if it is not stirred.
note: The barley drink falls apart unless stirred. Things hold together by moving.

q: Man kindles a light for himself in the night-time, when he has died but is alive. The sleeper, whose vision has been put out, lights up from the dead; he that is awake lights up from the sleeping.
note: Sleep touches death, waking touches sleep. Each state kindles from the one next to it.

q: Mortals are immortals and immortals are mortals, the one living the others’ death and dying the others’ life.
note: Life and death are woven together, all the way up to the gods.

q: The fool is fluttered at every word.
note: A fool is shaken by every word he hears. Steadiness is a sign of understanding.
